items.stem: Which statement most accurately expresses the critics’ claim, as distinct from a finding that is merely consistent with that claim?
choices: Residents who had already reported meeting neighbors were twice as likely to become weekly visitors.
Familiarity rose 14 percent in the courtyard blocks and 12 percent in the comparison blocks.
The courtyard blocks also received new streetlights during the study period.
The courtyards did not themselves broaden relationships; apparent effects may reflect the tendency of socially inclined residents to use them.
items.stimulus: In 2022, Harbor City converted six vacant lots into quiet courtyards with benches, shade trees, and no organized programming. Supporters claimed that these low-pressure spaces would increase neighbor familiarity by creating opportunities for casual encounters. Critics countered that any increase would reflect selection: people already inclined to linger would choose the courtyards, while the design itself would not change relationships. Researchers surveyed residents within three blocks of each lot before the conversions and one year afterward, comparing them with residents near matched lots scheduled for renovation the following year. Familiarity rose 14 percent in the courtyard blocks and 12 percent in the comparison blocks; meanwhile, the share of courtyard residents visiting weekly rose from 9 percent to 21 percent. Supporters noted that 63 percent of weekly visitors said they had met someone from another block, compared with 28 percent before the conversion. Critics replied that residents who had already reported meeting neighbors were twice as likely to become weekly visitors, and that the courtyard blocks also received new streetlights. A follow-up found that, among residents who had not met neighbors at the beginning, weekly courtyard visitors were no more likely to report a new acquaintance than nonvisitors in the comparison blocks. The study therefore establishes an association between courtyard use and encounters but does not establish that the courtyards themselves caused broader familiarity.

items.stem:
Engineer Sol Kwan argued that brightness was the primary cause of disruption and predicted that dimming either color would reduce the problem in roughly the same way. To test the competing claims, researchers installed adjustable fixtures at six previously unlit stretches and alternated their color and intensity each night. At high intensity, amber fixtures attracted 19 percent fewer moths than white fixtures, but at low intensity the two colors produced no significant difference in visits. Velez therefore narrowed her claim: color appeared to matter when light was bright enough to disrupt moths, not independently of intensity.

A six-month follow-up measured egg clusters rather than visits and found 11 percent more clusters near high-intensity amber fixtures than near high-intensity white ones; the two low-intensity conditions again did not differ. Because reed density could still influence egg-laying, researchers compared only stretches whose reed density changed similarly during the study. Amber still produced 7 percent more egg clusters in that comparison, but it involved only four stretches. The report consequently described amber lighting as a promising supplement to dimming, not a substitute for it: the color effect was conditional, and the evidence for a lasting reproductive benefit remained provisional.

Critics respond that young trees provide little shade at first and that irrigating them could consume scarce water. items.stem: Which finding from the passage most directly strengthens the organizers’ claim that access to the clinics, rather than the county’s general campaign, reduced appliance discards?
choices: Appliance discards fell 6 percent near clinics, compared with 2 percent elsewhere during the first year.
Neighborhoods without clinics nevertheless experienced a 4 percent decline after receiving the guide and rebate, while clinic neighborhoods retained their initial decline.
Most surveyed attendees said they would have discarded their items without the clinics.

items.stimulus: A county launched monthly Repair Saturdays, where volunteers fixed small appliances at no charge, and organizers claimed that the clinics reduced household waste rather than merely postponing purchases. During the first year, 312 households brought items to the clinics, 78 percent of those households reported that they would otherwise have discarded the items, and volunteers recorded 196 successful repairs. Because households chose whether to attend, however, these figures could not show how often nonattendees would have repaired or discarded comparable items. A county waste audit found that appliance discards fell 6 percent in neighborhoods within two miles of a clinic, compared with 2 percent in the rest of the county during the same year. Yet the county had also mailed a “maintain rather than replace” guide and offered a small rebate for delaying replacement, and the rebate was redeemed 1.5 times as often near clinics. In the second year, neighborhoods with clinics retained their initial decline, while neighborhoods that received the guide and rebate but had no clinic recorded a 4 percent decline. Organizers argued that this pattern showed clinic access added a distinct effect, although clinics were more often placed near libraries and transit stops. A critic replied that residents near those amenities might differ in income, mobility, or repair habits from residents elsewhere. To separate these possibilities, the county planned to compare future clinic sites with similar neighborhoods selected for libraries and transit but not yet scheduled to host clinics.

That pattern most directly supports an additional clinic effect.

items.stimulus:
Larkhaven replaced forty canal lamps with amber LEDs after residents complained that white light seemed to empty the paths of moths. items.stimulus:
At Marrow Point, Elian returned to the lighthouse to catalog the notebooks of Anja Venn, its keeper during the storm of 1978. His aunt Liora maintained that Anja had flashed a three-dark-one-bright pattern to guide fishing boats when the radio failed, but Bex, the retired harbor master, insisted that a damaged shutter had produced the pattern by accident. In Anja’s first notebook, Elian found a note that the west hinge “catches when wind comes hard,” followed by three short strokes and one long stroke in the margin. Because the marks recurred beside entries about rust, Elian initially took them for repair notation rather than a message.

On the next page, however, Anja had written, “I let the shutter rest between catches; the boats know the old rhythm.” The page was dated the night of the storm, though its ink had run where seawater had entered the room. Bex countered that the shutter had been replaced the following week, an expense that seemed unnecessary if Anja had been controlling it deliberately. In a box beneath the notebooks, Elian found a fisherman’s statement saying that he had seen the same rhythm from the reef before hearing the storm siren, although the statement had been written twenty years after the event.

When Elian showed Liora the page, she admitted that Anja sometimes copied ordinary mechanical patterns into her personal notebooks, yet she said Anja had once told her, “A light is only useless when nobody is watching.” Elian finally labeled the episode “probable warning, mechanism uncertain,” preserving both the repair invoice and the fisherman’s statement in the archive. He left the lighthouse without deciding whether Anja had commanded the shutter or merely recognized its failure, but he no longer believed that the boats’ safe return could be explained by the hinge alone.

His aunt Liora maintained that Anja had flashed a three-dark-one-bright pattern to guide fishing boats when the radio failed, but Bex, the retired harbor master, insisted that a damaged shutter had produced the pattern by accident. In Anja’s first notebook, Elian found a note that the west hinge “catches when wind comes hard,” followed by three short strokes and one long stroke in the margin. Because the marks recurred beside entries about rust, Elian initially took them for repair notation rather than a message.

On the next page, however, Anja had written, “I let the shutter rest between catches; the boats know the old rhythm.” The page was dated the night of the storm, though its ink had run where seawater had entered the room. Bex countered that the shutter had been replaced the following week, an expense that seemed unnecessary if Anja had been controlling it deliberately. In a box beneath the notebooks, Elian found a fisherman’s statement saying that he had seen the same rhythm from the reef before hearing the storm siren, although the statement had been written twenty years after the event.

When Elian showed Liora the page, she admitted that Anja sometimes copied ordinary mechanical patterns into her personal notebooks, yet she said Anja had once told her, “A light is only useless when nobody is watching.” Elian finally labeled the episode “probable warning, mechanism uncertain,” preserving both the repair invoice and the fisherman’s statement in the archive. He left the lighthouse without deciding whether Anja had commanded the shutter or merely recognized its failure, but he no longer believed that the boats’ safe return could be explained by the hinge alone.

items.stimulus:
At the harbor museum, four eighteenth-century tiled panels known as the Tide Gates have long been credited to Ivo Maran because each contains a blue gull. Historian Priya Sen argues that this catalog confuses recurrence with authorship: the gull was a workshop pattern, and the panels were likely assembled by several hands. The older attribution drew strength from the same cobalt pigment and consistent horizon line, but those features could reflect materials or a design supplied in advance.

Sen points to a 1738 guild inventory that calls Maran “designer of the Tide Gates” and lists payments separately to “tile setters”; she reads the wording as a division between conception and execution. Yet historian Tomas Vale notes that the inventory uses occupational labels inconsistently, and no setter is named. Conservation found that the gull’s wing angle changes at tile seams while the horizon remains level across panels, a pattern Sen says fits local adaptation of a template better than repeated freehand copying.
